input.question: If oral contraceptives prevent ovulation, why don't they also extend a woman's fertility?
input.ground_truth: A woman has thousands of eggs and its not like she can "go out" there are other bodily functions that makes it so that the eggs stops maturing after a certain age (sorry idont know exactly what causes it) and while she cant have more children she still got alot of eggs that simply wont mature and is beeing slowly absorbed by the body. So it does not matter if there are 20 eggs left or 10.000 eggs when menapause hits...

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If oral contraceptives prevent ovulation, why don't they also extend a woman's fertility?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body has a little clock that helps you grow up and have babies when you’re ready. Oral contraceptives are like a “stop” button for that little clock. They tell your body, “Not now, we don’t want an egg to come out this month.” That’s what “preventing ovulation” means—no egg comes out to meet a sperm.

But, just because the “stop” button is pressed for now, doesn’t mean your body forgets how to have a baby forever. When you stop taking the pill, your body’s clock can start working again. So, the pill doesn’t make you less able to have a baby in the future—it just pauses things for a while.

So, oral contraceptives stop eggs from coming out for a little while, but they don’t take away your ability to have a baby when you want to.
